Steamed watercress

Serves 4

Written for wild watercress (Nasturtium officinale) by an American chef.

Ingredients
  • 450 g (1 lb) fresh watercress
  • salt
  • soft salted butter or extra virgin olive oil
  • lemon wedges or vinegar, to serve
Method
  1. Wash the watercress, picking out insects and debris, and dry it well, ideally in a salad spinner.
  2. Put a thin film of water in a large pot, fill the pot with the watercress and cover it.
  3. Set it over medium-high heat for a few minutes until the pot is very hot, then lift the lid and stir.
  4. Cover again for a minute or two, stir, and repeat until the watercress has wilted.
  5. Keep cooking and tasting, adding a splash of water if it dries out, until it is tender: young shoots are quick, older leaves can take 15 minutes or more.
  6. Turn off the heat and pour off what little water is left.
  7. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil and salt, taste, and serve with lemon or a dash of vinegar, or butter at the table.

The author also steams it in a steamer basket over 5–8 cm of boiling water, covered on low heat, until tender, but prefers the pot method for watercress.

  • 125 g very cold butter
  • 250 g sieved plain flour
  • 50 g finely grated parmesan
  • 1 tsp icing sugar
  • salt
  • plenty of black pepper
  • just enough water
Filling
  • 500 g watercress leaves, with some white flowers kept for garnish
  • 20 g butter
  • the juice of 1 orange
  • 3 large eggs plus 2 extra yolks
  • 300 ml double cream
  • 200 g grated parmesan
  • salt and pepper
  • 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180 °C.
  2. For the pastry, grate 125 g very cold butter into 250 g sieved plain flour, 50 g finely grated parmesan, 1 tsp icing sugar, salt and plenty of black pepper.
  3. Rub together lightly, keeping it cool, then add just enough water to form a rough ball (less water, less shrinking).
  4. Chill for 30 minutes, roll out and line the tin, patching where needed.
  5. Prick the base, chill for 20 minutes, then blind-bake with baking paper and beans for 15 minutes; remove them and bake on until lightly toasted.
  6. For the filling, strip 500 g watercress leaves from the fibrous stalks (some stalk is fine — just a coarser tart), keeping some white flowers for garnish.
  7. Melt 20 g butter in a large heavy pan over a medium heat, add the watercress and the juice of 1 orange, and sweat gently for 10 minutes, stirring often.
  8. Blitz it with its juices, then beat it hard with 3 large eggs and 2 extra yolks, 300 ml double cream, all but a handful of 200 g grated parmesan, and plenty of salt and pepper — the more air, the more it rises.
  9. Pour into the case, sprinkle with the reserved parmesan and 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts, and bake for 20–25 minutes, until bronzed and only slightly wobbly in the middle.
  10. Cool a little and scatter the watercress flowers on top.

Method
  1. Split the pods into single seeds and rinse off any dirt.

  7. Use them wherever you would use capers.

  • a bowl of iced water

Method
  1. Bring the water to the boil and pour it over the flowers, pushing them under.
  2. Cover and steep for at least an hour, or overnight in the fridge.
  3. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing gently, and top up with water to 950 ml.
  4. Put this tea in a large pot with the lemon juice and whisk in the pectin until it dissolves.
  5. Bring to a full rolling boil over high heat, stirring all the time, and boil for 1 minute.
  6. Add all the sugar at once and stir to dissolve.
  7. Return to a full rolling boil and boil hard for exactly 1 minute.
  8. Take it off the heat and skim off the foam.
  9. Ladle into prepared jars, leaving 6 mm of headspace, wipe the rims, and put on the lids and bands fingertip-tight.
  10. Process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes, turn off the heat and leave the jars 5 minutes.
  11. Leave them undisturbed for 12–24 hours before checking the seals.

Baked butternut and nipplewort rice

Written for nipplewort picked in an English garden. The author gives no amounts — use what suits you: butternut squash, peeled and cubed; brown basmati rice; freshly picked nipplewort, chopped; onion and garlic; fresh sage and thyme; vegetable or mushroom stock; olive oil; salt and pepper.

Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180–200 °C and start the rice (for brown basmati, put it in cold salted water, bring it to the boil, then simmer 25–30 minutes; it can go into the oven part-cooked, with more stock, to finish).
  2. Toss the squash with olive oil in a large oven dish and roast it.
  3. When it starts to brown, stir in the chopped onion; when the onion turns translucent, add the garlic and herbs, taking care not to burn them.
  4. When the garlic just colours, add the nipplewort and some stock and cook about 5 minutes more, until the leaves wilt.
  5. Stir in the cooked rice and seasoning, with a little more stock if needed to moisten the rice rather than make soup, and return it to the oven until the rice is hot and has soaked up most of the liquid.
  6. Take out any herb stalks and serve.
  7. Mushrooms roasted with the squash, or chickpeas or other beans, go in well too.

Method

Oregon grape Berberis aquifolium 1 recipe

Oregon grape jelly

Written for Oregon grape (Mahonia aquifolium, or its low relative M. nervosa) by a preserving author in Oregon.

Ingredients
  • About 1.6 kg Oregon grape berries
  • water
  • about 450 g (2¼ cups) sugar
Method
  1. Pick about 1.6 kg berries once they are evenly dark; sliding your fingers down a bunch drops them into the basket.
  2. Simmer the berries, covered, with half their volume of water for 15 minutes, mashing them after the first 10.
  3. Let the juice drip through a jelly bag for several hours, then boil it for 10 minutes to reduce it a little.
  4. Combine about 720 ml (3 cups) juice with about 450 g (2¼ cups) sugar in a wide, heavy, non-reactive pan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves.
  5. Raise the heat and boil, skimming now and then, until it begins to jell, which takes only a few minutes: drops falling from a tipped metal spoon thicken and run together.
  6. Skim, pour into three sterilised half-pint (about 240 ml) jars and process in a boiling-water bath for 5 minutes; it should be firm by the next day.

The author advises against doubling the batch. Metric amounts are converted from the source's pounds and cups.

Method
  1. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks.

Method
  1. Heat the oven to 200 °C.

  3. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat.
  4. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts.

  6. Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.

Pineapple weed posset pots

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 30 g butter
  • 75 g digestive biscuits (about 6), crushed
  • 50 g pineapple weed flower heads
  • 300 ml double cream
  • 75 g caster sugar
  • 3 tablespoons lemon juice
Method
  1. Melt the butter over a gentle heat, take it off the heat and stir in the crushed biscuits; press the crumbs into the bottom of 4 small glasses or ramekins and chill for half an hour.
  2. Crush the flower heads thoroughly in a mortar and pestle (or in a bowl with a potato masher).
  3. Put the cream, crushed flower heads and sugar in a small pan over a medium heat and bring to the boil, stirring gently to dissolve the sugar, then lower the heat and simmer for 3 minutes.
  4. Take off the heat, whisk in the lemon juice, and strain through a fine sieve into a jug.
  5. Pour over the chilled bases, leave to cool, then chill for at least 3 hours.
  6. For the purest pineapple flavour, pick the flower heads carefully and leave out the leaves.

Pineapple weed ice cream

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • a bunch of pineapple weed (the more flowers, the sweeter the ice cream)
  • 250 ml double cream
  • 250 ml full-fat milk
  • 2 teaspoons honey
  • 250 ml Greek yoghurt
Method
  1. Chop the pineapple weed and put it in a pan with the cream, milk and honey.
  2. Bring to a simmer and simmer for 10 minutes, then leave to cool and infuse overnight.
  3. Warm it slightly so it runs, strain it through a sieve, and squeeze the stems to get out as much flavour as you can.
  4. Leave to cool and stir in the yoghurt.
  5. Churn in an ice cream maker for about 30 minutes, until frozen, or freeze it in a shallow tub and whisk it every 2 hours until smoothly frozen.

Ingredients

Method
  1. Put half the pineapple weed and the vodka in a glass jar, cover it and shake it, and keep it out of direct sun, shaking it once a day.

  3. Meanwhile, shake the other half of the pineapple weed with the sugar in a lidded container and leave it overnight.

Porcini on toast

View source recipe

Dried porcini and their stock

Ingredients
  • Fresh porcini
  • a food dehydrator
  • boiling water for soaking
Method
  1. Wipe the caps and stems clean with a damp cloth, without soaking them, as they can turn slimy.
  2. Peel off the brown cap skin if you prefer; if it won't come away easily, pull it off the slices after cutting.
  3. Slice no more than 6 mm thick and spread the slices on dehydrator racks.
  4. Dry at 55–60 °C for two to six hours, depending on how thin the slices are and how many racks you are running.
  5. Stop when they are light and brittle to slightly bendy, with nothing soft left.
  6. Let them cool to room temperature, then seal them in a jar or airtight container and keep them out of the light.
  7. To use, cover a handful with boiling water.
  8. Use both the softened porcini and their soaking broth in risotto, pasta, sauces and other savoury dishes.
  9. You can also drop the dried slices straight into a sauce or stew and let its liquid soften them.

The author finds dried porcini keep for at least one to two years.

Ultimate wild mushroom risotto

Serves 4

Written for mixed wild mushrooms — the author's are dried porcini (cep), puffball and chanterelles.

Ingredients
  • 2 litres of good chicken or vegetable stock
  • 30 g dried porcini
  • 150 g chanterelles
  • 1 finely diced large onion
  • 3 garlic cloves
  • 3 bay leaves
  • 1 courgette, finely diced
  • 1 small leek, finely diced
  • 100 g butter
  • a few sprigs of thyme
  • 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice
  • 300 ml dry white wine
  • 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes
  • salt and pepper
  • 300 g finely grated parmesan
  • 75 ml double cream
  • a handful of finely chopped parsley and tarragon
  • the juice of 1 lemon
  • truffle oil
  • hairy bittercress (optional)
Method
  1. Heat 2 litres of good chicken or vegetable stock in a separate pan and add 30 g dried porcini to soak and enrich it.
  2. Sweat 150 g chanterelles in a frying pan until they give up their juice, and strain the juice into the stock.
  3. In a heavy pan, sweat 1 finely diced large onion, 3 garlic cloves, 3 bay leaves, and 1 courgette and 1 small leek (both finely diced) in 50 g of 100 g butter until soft and translucent.
  4. Add a few sprigs of thyme and 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice and stir over a medium heat for a couple of minutes.
  5. Add 300 ml dry white wine and keep stirring as it absorbs.
  6. Add 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes, and the soaked porcini with a little hot stock.
  7. Keep stirring briskly, adding the stock a ladleful at a time; when about half is in, add the chanterelles.
  8. Season, and stop when the rice keeps a hint of bite (no chalkiness) and the risotto is like a very thick soup — you may not need all the stock.
  9. Off the heat, stir in half of 300 g finely grated parmesan, the remaining 50 g butter, 75 ml double cream and a handful of finely chopped parsley and tarragon.
  10. Cover and rest for a few minutes.
  11. Stir in the juice of 1 lemon, check the seasoning and add a little more stock if needed.
  12. Serve in shallow bowls with a few drops of truffle oil, the rest of the cheese on the side, and, if you like, a sprinkle of hairy bittercress for a sharp note.

  • butter or oil
  • 200 g finely grated parmesan or another strong hard cheese
  • up to 500 g cream cheese
  • a large handful of sorrel leaves or a squeeze of lemon juice
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Use 1 kg fresh mushrooms, or 250 g dried (soaked for 30 minutes in boiling water and drained), or a mix.
  2. Chop roughly and cook thoroughly in butter or oil over a medium heat until all the moisture has gone (the juice can be strained off as a mushroom broth).
  3. Cool, then squeeze out any remaining moisture.
  4. Blend in a food processor, then add 200 g finely grated parmesan or another strong hard cheese, up to 500 g cream cheese (less for a more mushroomy pâté), a large handful of sorrel leaves or a squeeze of lemon juice, and salt and pepper, in stages, tasting as you go.
  5. Optional extras: dried porcini powder cooked with the mushrooms, black garlic, finely chopped pickled walnuts stirred through at the end, miso, soy sauce or dried seaweed powder.
  6. Pack into small tubs and label each with the species you used.

Keeps for a week in the fridge, or freeze it.

Pickled sow thistle buds

Ingredients
  • About 30 ml (⅛ cup) sow thistle flower buds

Method
  1. Snap off the top of each stem just below the cluster of buds and strip the leaves.

Pōhutukawa Metrosideros excelsa 1 recipe

Pōhutukawa fizzy drink

Makes 2.5 litres

Ingredients
  • 1 litre (4 cups) pōhutukawa stamens (stripped from the flowers)
  • 250 ml (1 cup) crushed strawberries
  • the flowers of 1 elderflower head (optional)
  • 375 ml (1½ cups) golden sugar
  • 1 sliced lemon
  • 2.5 litres water
Method
  1. The fizz comes from the wild yeasts on the flowers and strawberries, so use spray-free strawberries and don't wash either; keep as much of the pollen as you can when picking.
  2. Stir the sugar, water and lemon in a large jar until the sugar dissolves, then add the stamens, elderflowers and strawberries and push them under.
  3. Cover with muslin held by a rubber band, and date it.
  4. Stir hard every day for 3–4 days; it is fermenting when the flowers rise and bubbles appear as you stir.
  5. Strain through muslin into flip-top bottles and leave at room temperature for 1–2 days, checking the fizz, then refrigerate once it is as fizzy as you like.
  6. Serve cold; the cold slows the fermentation, so it keeps a long time in the fridge.

Radish kraut

Makes about 400 g

Ingredients
  • 300 g radishes, washed and finely sliced
  • ½ red pepper, finely chopped
  • 10 ml (2 tsp) sea salt
  • 2.5 ml (½ tsp) demerara sugar
  • 2 crushed garlic cloves
  • 1 red chilli, deseeded and finely chopped
  • still mineral water, if needed
Method
  1. Sterilise a jar first, and plan to check the ferment every day for 4–5 days.
  2. In a bowl, combine 300 g radishes, washed and finely sliced (a mandolin is best), and ½ red pepper, finely chopped, with 10 ml (2 tsp) sea salt and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) demerara sugar, and scrunch them hard with your hands to start the juices running.
  3. Leave for 1 hour, then squeeze again for about 10 minutes.
  4. Add 2 crushed garlic cloves and 1 red chilli, deseeded and finely chopped, and squeeze some more.
  5. Pack it into the jar, pressing down hard (the end of a clean rolling pin works) so there are no air pockets and the brine covers the vegetables, leaving 2–3 cm of space at the top.
  6. If the brine does not cover them, top up with still mineral water — they must be fully under liquid.
  7. Push a scrunched piece of baking paper firmly down on top to keep them under, cover with clean muslin held on with a rubber band, and leave on a cool, dark shelf for 4–7 days, to taste; it ferments faster when warm, slower when cold.
  8. Each day, lift off the muslin and paper to check it and let the gas escape, then cover it again.
  9. When it tastes right, take out the paper and muslin, put the lid on and refrigerate to stop the ferment; it keeps for months.
  10. Use it in salads, hot dogs and burgers.

Apple and rose geranium jelly

Makes about eight 250 ml jars

Ingredients
  • About 125 ml fresh rose geranium leaves and tender stems, firmly packed
  • 750 ml apple juice
  • one packet of powdered fruit pectin
  • 1.2 kg sugar
Method
  1. Firmly pack about 125 ml of fresh rose geranium leaves and tender stems.
  2. Bring them to the boil with part of 750 ml apple juice, take off the heat and steep for at least 15–20 minutes.
  3. Strain, add the rest of the juice and top up to 750 ml if needed.

  6. Take off the heat, skim off the foam quickly and pour at once into sterilised jars — a whole leaf can be pressed into each jar.
  7. Seal and process for 5 minutes in a hot water bath, following the jar maker's instructions.

  3. In a large bowl mix about 150 g brown sugar, 2 tablespoons cornflour and the grated rind of the two oranges, tip in the rhubarb and mix well.
  4. Grease the dish and spread the rhubarb mixture back into it.
  5. Strain the juice over it.
  6. For the topping, mix about 150 g brown sugar, about 90 g whole rolled oats, about 90 g fine rolled oats and about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds), then rub in 2 tablespoons soft butter.
  7. Press the topping firmly over the rhubarb and around the edges.
  8. Bake at 180 °C for 45 minutes.

Rose geranium sugar

Method
  1. Fill a dry glass jar with alternate layers of rose geranium leaves and caster sugar.

View source recipe

Rose geranium lemonade

Ingredients
  • 250 ml water
  • 200 g sugar
  • 10 clean rose geranium leaves
  • 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice
  • chilled water and ice, to serve
  • a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals, to garnish
Method
  1. Boil 250 ml water with 200 g sugar in a small pot.
  2. Take off the heat, add 10 clean rose geranium leaves and leave until cold, overnight if you can.
  3. Squeeze the leaves out well (repeat with fresh leaves for a stronger flavour).
  4. Add 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice, bottle and refrigerate; it keeps for up to two weeks.
  5. To serve, stir 1 tablespoon of the concentrate into each cup of chilled water and pour over ice, garnished with a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals.

View source recipe

Rose geranium shortbread

Makes 8 wedges

Ingredients
  • About 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter
  • about 60 g icing sugar
  • about 190 g plain flour
  • ¼ teaspoon salt
  • 1 teaspoon rose water
  • 8 large rose geranium leaves, washed and dried
  • 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar)
  • fresh rose geranium leaves, to serve
Method
  1. Cream about 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter with about 60 g icing sugar until light and fluffy.
  2. Mix about 190 g plain flour with ¼ teaspoon salt, add it to the butter, then mix in 1 teaspoon rose water.
  3. Gather into a ball, wrap and refrigerate for 4–6 hours.
  4. Let it soften a little.
  5. Butter and flour the base of a 20 cm round tin.
  6. On baking paper, pat the dough out to the size of the tin.
  7. Press 8 large, washed and dried rose geranium leaves into the dough in a circle about 2.5 cm in from the edge, lay the dough in the tin leaf side down and pat it out to the edges.
  8. Score it lightly into 8 wedges, sprinkle with 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar) and chill for 45 minutes.
  9. Bake at 160 °C for about 20 minutes, until it just starts to colour.
  10. Cool in the tin, turn out, peel the baked leaves off the base, cut along the marks and serve with fresh rose geranium leaves.

Scented geranium and lemon icing

Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named.

Ingredients
  • 2–3 scented geranium leaves
  • about 250 g sifted icing sugar
  • a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese
  • 2 teaspoons softened butter
  • 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind
  • lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel, to decorate (optional)
Method
  1. Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl.
  2. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces.
  3. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth.
  4. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.

Pineapple and rose geranium ice

Written for "rose-scented geranium" leaves without naming a species.

  • 1 litre pineapple juice
  • 10 rose-scented geranium leaves
  • 400 g sugar

Method
  1. Warm 1 litre pineapple juice slightly, add 10 rose-scented geranium leaves and bruise them gently against the side of the container with a spoon.

Rose geranium cream

Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species.

  • 300 ml fresh cream
  • 4 tablespoons caster sugar
  • 4–6 rose-scented geranium leaves
  • 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed)

Method
  1. Heat 300 ml fresh cream, 4 tablespoons caster sugar and 4–6 rose-scented geranium leaves in a pot, stirring often, until just short of boiling; do not let it boil.

Rowan tree Sorbus aucuparia 4 recipes

Rowan bud syrup

Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts.

Ingredients
  • Young rowan flower buds and very young leaf buds
  • cold water
  • 100 g sugar per 100 ml of water, or up to twice that
  • 10% vodka (optional)
Method
  1. Put young rowan flower buds and very young leaf buds in a pan and cover them with cold water, measuring the water.
  2. Add 100 g sugar per 100 ml of water, or up to twice that for a thicker syrup that keeps better.
  3. Heat, stirring to dissolve the sugar, and hold it at about 70 °C for a few minutes; the author simmers for no more than 5 minutes, as the almond flavour fades fast with heat.
  4. Leave to cool and strain into sterilised bottles, keeping the syrupy buds for the liqueur.
  5. Add 10% vodka to help it keep, or store it in the fridge, or freeze it in plastic bottles.

View source recipe

Rowan bud liqueur

Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts.

Ingredients
  • The syrup-coated buds left from the rowan bud syrup
  • cheap vodka
  • rowan bud syrup, to taste
Method
  1. Put the syrup-coated buds left from the rowan bud syrup in a jar, cover with cheap vodka and leave for about 4 weeks, shaking now and then.
  2. Strain, then sweeten to taste with the rowan bud syrup — the author aims for about 20–25% alcohol.

Adding more fresh buds to the vodka strengthens the almond flavour, but also extracts more of the cyanogenic glycoside; the author says to drink correspondingly less.

Method
  1. To clean them first, soak them in 1.4 litres of water with 120 ml white vinegar.

  • 400 g caps sliced
  • 4 cloves garlic chopped
  • oil
  • 80 ml white wine
  • 125 g cream cheese
  • 3 tbsp sour cream
  • 2 sage leaves
  • 2 sprigs thyme
  • salt and pepper
  • 1 sheet butter puff pastry
  • 1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tsp water
Method
  1. Fry the garlic a minute in oil over medium heat, add the mushrooms and cook 5 minutes, adding oil as they take it.
  2. Stir in the wine, cream cheese, sour cream, sage and thyme and cook until creamy and tender, then season and cool completely — this can be done a day ahead.
  3. Heap the filling down the centre of the pastry sheet, seal the edges with the egg wash, press the ends with a fork, and bake at 220 °C for 30 minutes until golden.

  • parsley
Method
  1. Fry the onion and garlic in oil a few minutes until translucent, melt the butter into them, then stir in the flour.
  2. Add the mushrooms, paprika and stock and simmer about 10 minutes until the mushrooms are done.

Saffron milk cap risotto

Ingredients
  • 125 ml olive oil
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 300 g caps with the stems off and thinly sliced
  • 3 sprigs thyme
  • an onion
  • 105 g arborio rice
  • 1 litre chicken stock
  • a pinch of saffron
  • 165 ml dry white wine
  • 125 ml cream
  • 25 g blue cheese
  • chopped chives or parsley, to serve
Method
  1. Sauté the mushrooms in half the oil with the butter over medium-high until coated, season, and set aside.
  2. Soften the diced onion in the rest of the oil over medium heat for 5–8 minutes without browning, while the stock warms with the saffron in another pan.
  3. Stir the rice through the onion, then add the hot stock a ladle at a time, letting each one absorb, for 15–20 minutes until the rice is cooked.
  4. Stir in the wine, blue cheese and cream, fold through half the mushrooms, and season.
  5. Plate it with the remaining mushrooms on top and chopped chives or parsley.

Saffron milk cap and ash brie tart

Ingredients
Pastry
  • 480 g plain flour
  • 150 g cold cubed butter
  • 240 ml finely grated parmesan
  • 2.5 ml fine salt
  • 1 egg
  • 120–160 ml ice water
Filling
  • 5 caps
  • 4 cloves garlic sliced
  • olive oil
  • 150 g ash brie sliced
  • 3 eggs
  • 240 ml cream
  • 240 ml parmesan
  • 2 sprigs thyme
Method
  1. Clean the mushrooms in 1.4 litres of water with 120 ml white vinegar.
  2. Pulse the flour, butter, cheese and salt in a food processor, add the egg and 120 ml water and run it until it starts to come together, then knead on a floured bench with more water if it needs it and rest it 30 minutes at room temperature.
  3. Line an oiled 31 × 21 cm loose-bottomed tart tin, trim, and chill 45 minutes or freeze 15.
  4. Meanwhile fry the garlic then the mushrooms — whole if small, sliced if not — in oil over medium heat only until they keep their bright orange, then season and cool a little.
  5. Blind bake at 200 °C under oiled foil and weights for 20 minutes, then 10–15 minutes uncovered.
  6. Drop the oven to 150 °C, whisk the eggs, cream and parmesan, pour it into the case, arrange the mushrooms and brie on top with the thyme, and bake 30–35 minutes until just set.
  7. Serve warm.

Pan-fried snapper with sautéed sea parsley and warrigal greens

Serves 2

Written for sea parsley (Apium prostratum var. prostratum) sold by a Western Australian native-plant nursery; the recipe is by RiverMint Dining.

Ingredients
  • 350 g skin-on snapper fillets, scaled (keep the bones)
  • 100 g warrigal greens
  • 200 ml vegetable purée, such as turnip, potato or pea
  • 150 g cold butter, cubed
  • 2 sticks celery
  • half an onion, roughly chopped
  • 3 lemons
  • 20 sprigs dried native lemongrass
  • 3 sprigs sea parsley
  • salt and pepper
  • olive oil
Method
  1. Season and dry the fillets and fry them skin side down in hot olive oil for 2 minutes, pressing down so they don't shrink; turn and cook 2 minutes more.
  2. Add a squeeze of lemon and 15 ml (1 Tbsp) butter to the pan, baste, then keep the fish warm in a low oven.
  3. For the sauce, put the juice of a lemon, 10 lemongrass sprigs, the snapper bones, onion and celery in a pan, cover with water, bring to the boil and simmer 15 minutes, skimming.
  4. Strain out the bones, return to the pan and reduce by half, adding more lemongrass to taste; season and strain again.
  5. Over medium heat, whisk in the cold butter a few cubes at a time until the sauce thickens.
  6. Bash the warrigal greens with a rolling pin, boil them for 2 minutes to remove oxalic acid, then drain and squeeze dry.
  7. Blanch the sea parsley on its stems for 15 seconds so it keeps its crunch, refresh in iced water, then pick and dry the leaves and season them.
  8. Sauté the sea parsley and warrigal greens in hot butter.
  9. Spread the purée on the plates, top with the greens and the snapper, crisp skin up, drizzle with the lemongrass sauce and garnish with the sea parsley.
  10. Warrigal greens are New Zealand spinach, which is At Risk in the wild in New Zealand; use cultivated ones.

Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

Ingredients
  • 2 cloves garlic, minced
  • olive oil for cooking
  • 2 spring onions, chopped
  • 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock
  • 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish
  • 3 medium mint leaves
  • 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks.

Sorrel soup

Serves 4 as a side

Written for sheep sorrel (adapted from Anja Dunk's sorrel soup).

Ingredients
  • 80–100 g sheep sorrel leaves (about 4 handfuls)
  • 60 g spinach leaves (2 large handfuls)
  • 40 g butter
  • 30 g plain flour
  • about 1 litre hot vegetable stock
  • 2 tbsp neutral oil
  • salt and black pepper
Method
  1. Put 80–100 g sheep sorrel leaves (about 4 handfuls) and 60 g spinach leaves (2 large handfuls) in a bowl of water, swish them about, let the dirt settle, then lift them out and dry them.
  2. In a saucepan over a medium heat, melt 40 g butter, add 30 g plain flour and stir for 3 minutes, until light tan.
  3. Whisk in about 1 litre of hot vegetable stock in a slow stream, then barely simmer for 10 minutes, until thickened.
  4. Meanwhile heat 2 tbsp neutral oil in a frying pan and wilt the greens for 60 seconds (the sorrel turns yellowish).
  5. Stir the greens into the soup, blend, and season with salt and black pepper.

Spear-leaved orache Atriplex prostrata 1 recipe

Pine-fired mussels with orache

Serves 4

Written for spear-leaved orache, this plant.

Ingredients
  • 2 kg mussels, cleaned and de-bearded (foraged ones need thorough cleaning and checking)
  • a basket of very dry pine needles
  • malted barley, enough to cover the tray
  • a splash of whisky (the source uses Bowmore 12 Years Old)
  • 1 garlic clove
  • 2 handfuls of orache leaves
  • a knob of butter
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) olive oil
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Outside, scatter a layer of malted barley over a large metal tray, about 40–50 cm across.
  2. Lay the mussels hinge side up, side by side, in a big circle, and pile pine needles about 20 cm high over them.
  3. Light the needles in several places, upwind of the tray, and blow on them to get them going; the fire is dramatic, so choose the spot with care.
  4. When the needles have burnt down, after 5–10 minutes, pick the mussels out of their shells, carefully, as the shells can be hot.
  5. Heat the butter, olive oil and garlic in a pan over a medium heat for 1 minute, add the orache, cover and cook for 2–3 minutes.
  6. Add the mussels, season with salt and pepper and heat through.
  7. Mussels must be properly cooked: if in any doubt, bring them to a simmer and cook for 2 minutes.
  8. Serve in clean oyster shells.

The source lists the whisky but its method never says where it goes, and it uses the malted barley without listing it.

Stinging nettle Urtica dioica 15 recipes

Nettle pesto

Makes 1 jar

Ingredients
  • 50 g walnuts
  • 50 g nettle leaves (weighed after picking)
  • 20 g pine nuts
  • 2 garlic cloves, minced
  • 30 g basil (stalks and all)
  • the juice of 1 lemon
  • salt and black pepper
  • 125–175 ml extra virgin olive oil
Method
  1. Roast 50 g walnuts at 180 °C (fan) for 7–8 minutes, until lightly browned, and let them cool.
  2. Wearing gloves, pick the leaves off the nettles, discard the thick stalks and wash the leaves well.
  3. Blanch 50 g of leaves (weighed after picking) in boiling salted water for 20–30 seconds, until just wilted, lift them into iced water, then squeeze out as much water as you can — they no longer sting.
  4. Blend the walnuts and nettles with 20 g pine nuts, 2 minced garlic cloves, 30 g basil (stalks and all), the juice of 1 lemon, salt and black pepper, drizzling in 125–175 ml extra virgin olive oil until almost smooth.

Keeps up to a week in an airtight jar in the fridge.

View source recipe

Nettle beer

Makes 6 × 750 ml bottles

Ingredients
  • 1 kg nettle tops
  • 4 litres water
  • 750 g sugar
  • the juice of 1 lemon
  • 25 g cream of tartar
  • a sachet of ale yeast
Method
  1. Sterilise everything first — pots, demijohn, bottles and siphon tube.
  2. Wash and drain 1 kg nettle tops.
  3. Bring 4 litres of water to the boil, add the nettles, boil hard for 15 minutes, then strain into a clean pot.
  4. Stir in 750 g sugar, the juice of 1 lemon and 25 g cream of tartar until dissolved, and leave to cool to room temperature.
  5. Sprinkle a sachet of ale yeast over the surface, cover with muslin or a tea towel and leave overnight.
  6. Next day pour it into a demijohn with a bung and airlock and leave to ferment for up to 6 days.
  7. Siphon into brown bottles, cap them and chill in the fridge for a week before drinking.

Classic stinging nettle soup

Serves 6

Written for common stinging nettle (Urtica dioica and similar nettles) in North America.

Ingredients
  • About 225 g nettles
  • 1 cup diced celery
  • 2 cups diced leeks
  • 2 diced shallots
  • 1 small diced onion
  • 3 tbsp butter
  • about 1 litre chicken stock
  • 2 cups diced potato
  • 120 ml cream
  • salt and white pepper
  • crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint, to serve
Method
  1. Blanch about 225 g nettles in salted boiling water until just wilted, about 30 seconds, cool them in cold water, squeeze dry and finely chop a handful to finish the soup.
  2. Sweat 1 cup diced celery, 2 cups diced leeks, 2 diced shallots and 1 small diced onion in 3 tbsp butter over medium heat for 5 minutes.
  3. Add about 1 litre chicken stock and 2 cups diced potato and simmer until tender, about 15 minutes.
  4. Add the blanched nettles and blend, then stir in the chopped nettles and 120 ml cream and season with salt and white pepper.
  5. Serve with crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint.

Steamed nettles with ricotta

Serves 2

Written for common stinging nettle (Urtica dioica and similar nettles) in North America.

Ingredients
  • About 225 g young nettle tops
  • 3 large garlic cloves, crushed
  • 3 tbsp olive oil, plus more to serve
  • salt and pepper
  • a pinch of chilli flakes
  • ½ cup ricotta
  • lemon wedges, to serve
Method
  1. Wash about 225 g young nettle tops and steam them, covered, over boiling water for 2–3 minutes until tender.
  2. Meanwhile warm 3 large crushed garlic cloves in 3 tbsp olive oil over medium heat for at least 10 minutes until browned, then discard the garlic.
  3. Add the steamed nettles to the oil, season with salt, pepper and a pinch of chilli flakes, gently fold in ½ cup ricotta and warm through.
  4. Serve warm or at room temperature with olive oil and lemon wedges.

Nettle spanakopita

Serves 6

Written for stinging nettle in Britain; the recipe does not name the species.

Ingredients
  • 25 g butter
  • 150 g nettle leaves, washed
  • 200 g feta, crumbled
  • 50 g parmesan, grated
  • the zest and juice of a lemon
  • 1 egg, beaten
  • grated nutmeg
  • seasoning
  • 7 filo sheets
  • 75 g melted butter
  • 1 tbsp sesame seeds
Method
  1. Brown 25 g butter in a large frying pan, add 150 g washed, still-damp nettle leaves and cook for about 6 minutes until wilted; cool, squeeze out the liquid and chop roughly.
  2. Mix with 200 g crumbled feta, 50 g grated parmesan, the zest and juice of a lemon, two-thirds of a beaten egg, grated nutmeg and seasoning.
  3. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan).
  4. Lay 3 filo sheets end to end, overlapping by about 5 cm, brush with some of 75 g melted butter, add 3 more sheets and more butter, then a seventh sheet in the middle.
  5. Spoon the filling in a line about 2 cm wide along one long edge, tuck in the ends, roll into a long sausage and coil it into a spiral about 20 cm across in a shallow round pan or on a buttered baking tray.
  6. Brush with the rest of the egg, scatter with 1 tbsp sesame seeds and bake for 40–45 minutes until golden.

Nettle frittata

Serves 6

Written for common stinging nettle (Urtica dioica and similar nettles) in North America.

Ingredients
  • About 450 g tender nettle tops
  • 3 tbsp melted butter
  • 60 ml cream, warmed
  • ¼ tsp salt
  • black pepper
  • a little grated nutmeg
  • 4 large eggs
  • 1 tbsp oil
  • 3 tbsp grated parmesan
  • a little tomato sauce, to serve
Method
  1. Steam about 450 g tender nettle tops for at least 5 minutes, until thoroughly wilted, in batches if your pot is small.
  2. Chop them finely and, while still warm, mix in 3 tbsp melted butter, 60 ml warmed cream, ¼ tsp salt, black pepper and a little grated nutmeg, then work in 4 large eggs — the mixture will look stiff.
  3. Heat the grill.
  4. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a 20 cm cast-iron pan until nearly smoking, pack the mixture in and press it down, cover, turn the heat to medium and cook for 5 minutes.

  6. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting into wedges; good with a little tomato sauce.

Nettle and breadcrumb gnocchi

Serves 4 as a starter

Written for common stinging nettle (Urtica dioica and similar nettles) in North America.

Ingredients
  • About 115 g nettles, washed
  • 1 egg
  • 2 egg yolks
  • ½ cup grated parmesan, plus more to serve
  • a little nutmeg

  • ¾ cup (about 85 g) fine dry breadcrumbs, plus more if needed
  • flour for dusting
  • 4 tbsp butter
  • 1½ tbsp thinly sliced mint
  • salt and pepper
  • 60 ml dry white wine
  • about 1 cup warm tomato sauce
Method
  1. Steam about 115 g washed nettles for 2–3 minutes, spread them on a tray to cool, then chop roughly and purée in a food processor with 1 egg, 2 egg yolks, ½ cup grated parmesan, a little nutmeg and a pinch of salt.
  2. Mix in ¾ cup (about 85 g) fine dry breadcrumbs, cover and rest for an hour; the dough should be firm, not sticky — knead in more crumbs if it is.
  3. With floured hands roll it into 1 cm logs, cut them on the diagonal and dust with flour (they can be frozen at this point).
  4. Boil in lightly salted water until they float, then a couple of minutes more, 3–5 minutes in all.
  5. Meanwhile brown 4 tbsp butter in a frying pan, add 1½ tbsp thinly sliced mint with salt and pepper for 20 seconds, then 60 ml dry white wine, and take it off the heat.
  6. Toss the gnocchi in the butter and serve on warm tomato sauce (about 1 cup) with grated parmesan.

Dock, dandelion and nettle puddings

Makes about 35 small puddings or one large one

Written for broad-leaved dock and dandelion, with stinging nettle as a swap for them (pick only the top six or so leaves, before the nettle flowers) and dried nettle in the coating.

Ingredients
  • 400 g pearl barley
  • 4 eggs, for hard-boiling
  • 2 large leeks
  • a little oil
  • about half a supermarket bag of dock and dandelion leaves, washed
  • 3 raw eggs, plus 1–2 more if needed
  • seasoning
  • flour
  • 1 beaten egg
  • 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs
  • 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle (optional)
  • garlic mayonnaise, to serve
Method
  1. Boil 400 g pearl barley until tender, drain and cool.
  2. Hard-boil 4 eggs and chop finely.
  3. Finely chop 2 large leeks and soften them in a little oil.
  4. Blanch about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves in boiling water for 20 seconds, then plunge into iced water (skip this and the puddings are more bitter and less green); squeeze out every drop of water and chop finely.
  5. Mix the chopped eggs, leeks, barley and greens with 3 raw eggs, and season very well.
  6. Wrap the mixture tightly in a tray covered with cling film, set in a larger tray of hot water, or seal it in a pudding bowl with baking paper, foil and string and stand it in a pan of water reaching at least halfway up.
  7. Steam for 45–60 minutes, in a 160 °C oven or on the hob, until it holds together; if it won't roll into balls, mix in 1–2 more raw eggs and steam longer.
  8. Turn out and serve as one pudding, or roll into small balls while warm and chill them (they freeze individually at this stage).
  9. Roll the chilled balls in flour, then in 1 beaten egg, then in 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs (mixed, if you like, with 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle), and deep-fry for 1–2 minutes until browned; or simply flour and fry them.
  10. Serve warm, with garlic mayonnaise.

Nettle cordial

Ingredients
  • Water and white sugar in equal parts (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar)
  • at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of nettle tops, pressed down, or more
  • citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar (optional)
Method
  1. Make a syrup of equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar), heating gently and stirring until the sugar dissolves.
  2. Add a load of nettle tops — the top 3 or 4 pairs of leaves and their stem, picked with gloves — at least a cupful (about 250 ml) pressed down, or more.
  3. Keep it on the heat until steaming hot, but don't let it boil.
  4. Leave to cool, then strain out the nettles (the author dries them in a dehydrator as nettle sweets).
  5. Stir in small amounts of citric acid or lemon juice until it tastes slightly sharp — or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar — or leave it as a syrup.

It keeps for several weeks in the fridge. The recipe works with dried nettles too, with a slightly different flavour.

Nettle gimlet

Method

Nettle and potato soup

Written for nettles: the author eats both perennial and annual (dwarf) nettle, and gives this soup from Richard Mabey's Food for Free (1972).

Ingredients
  • 4 large handfuls of nettle tops, picked with gloves
  • 1 large onion
  • 50 g butter or coconut oil
  • 2 potatoes
  • 1 litre vegetable stock
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) crème fraîche or yoghurt
  • salt, pepper and grated nutmeg
Method
  1. Strip the nettles from the thicker stalks and wash them.
  2. Melt the butter and cook the chopped onion gently until translucent.
  3. Add the nettles and the chopped potatoes and cook 2–3 minutes, then add the stock and simmer 20 minutes, crushing the potatoes now and then with a wooden spoon.
  4. Season, with a little grated nutmeg, and finish with a swirl of crème fraîche or yoghurt; blend it first if you want a smoother soup.

Spring clean smoothie

The author's greens, picked in spring, were cleavers, chickweed, herb Robert, stinging nettle (the page does not say which nettle), onion weed, speedwell, pūhā and lemon balm; she gives no amounts for them. She blends the nettle raw; the nettle page says to cook it, so blanch it first.

Method
  1. Chop the greens into the blender with 2 cabbage leaves, stalks removed, the juice of 1 large grapefruit, 125 ml (½ cup) kombucha and 500 ml (2 cups) water, and blend until the greens are broken down.
  2. Add 2 small bananas or 1 large, 1 apple, 1 kiwifruit (hairs scrubbed off, top and bottom trimmed), 1 whole orange, and 15 ml (1 tbsp) chia seeds and 5 ml (1 tsp) pumpkin seeds ground in a coffee grinder, and blend again.
  3. Decorate it with onion weed and viola flowers and a piece of orange.

Supplejack Ripogonum scandens 1 recipe

Kareao shoots with kawakawa-lemon emulsion and confit yolk

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 20 young kareao shoots, cut crosswise on an angle
  • 20 kawakawa leaves, blanched and squeezed of excess water
  • 1 lemon, zested and juiced
  • 250 g brown butter, melted
  • 6 egg yolks
  • 1 tbsp boiling water
  • 250 ml (1 cup) canola oil for the yolks, plus a little for frying
  • sea salt
Method
  1. Warm the 250 ml of oil in a small saucepan to just above body temperature, slip in 4 of the yolks and hold the oil at that temperature until serving; add a spare yolk or two in case any break.
  2. Blend the other 2 yolks at high speed for 10 seconds, add the boiling water and blend 20 seconds more.
  3. With the motor running, drizzle in the brown butter very slowly so the sauce thickens without splitting.
  4. Add the kawakawa, lemon zest and juice and blend until bright green and smooth, then season with salt.
  5. Heat a frying pan until hot, add a little oil and then the kareao, and sauté until just tender; season with salt.
  6. Spread 3 tbsp of the emulsion into a circle about 5 cm across in the middle of each plate.
  7. Lift the yolks from the oil with a slotted spoon, dab off the oil, set one in the centre of each circle with a pinch of salt and arrange the shoots around it.

Sweet chestnut Castanea sativa 4 recipes

Roasted sweet chestnuts

Ingredients
  • Fresh sweet chestnuts
  • melted butter
  • salt
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 220 °C.
  2. Prick or score each shell so the nuts cannot burst, spread them on a baking tray and flick a few drops of water over them with your fingers.
  3. Roast on the bottom shelf for 10 minutes, then turn them so they roast evenly and carry on until cooked, when the kernel peels away easily.
  4. Peel, dip in melted butter and salt to taste.

View source recipe

Chestnut flour

Ingredients
  • Fresh sweet chestnuts
  • a steamer
  • a coarse sieve
  • 500 g resealable freezer bags
Method
  1. Leave freshly gathered nuts somewhere dry for a few days to sweeten.
  2. On a chopping board, cut off the base and brown skin of each nut with a sharp knife, throwing out any that show signs of rot.
  3. Steam them for about 20 minutes.
  4. While they are hot, push them a few at a time through a coarse sieve with the end of a rolling pin to remove the brown inner skin; if they are very hard to push through, they need more steaming.
  5. The sieving dries them to a breadcrumb-like texture.
  6. Pack into 500 g resealable bags and freeze, and thaw before baking or cooking.

The author uses frozen processed chestnuts within six months, and finds a 500 g bag does a couple of meals for two.

Chestnut soup

Serves 4

Written for chestnuts in Britain; the page does not name the species.

Ingredients
  • 3 tbsp olive oil, plus extra to finish
  • 15 g butter
  • 1 medium onion, chopped
  • 6 sage leaves, roughly chopped, plus extra to finish
  • 1 small garlic clove, finely chopped
  • 1 litre vegetable stock
  • 400 g cooked, peeled chestnuts
  • 100 ml crème fraîche
  • sea salt and black pepper
Method
  1. Warm 1 tbsp of the oil with the butter over medium-low heat and soften the onion for about 10 minutes until translucent.
  2. Stir in the sage and garlic for a minute.
  3. Add the stock and all but a handful of the chestnuts, season, raise the heat and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring now and then.
  4. Cool slightly and blend until very smooth.
  5. Return to the pan, stir in the crème fraîche, adjust the seasoning and warm through gently without letting it boil.
  6. Slice the reserved chestnuts.
  7. Fry the extra sage leaves in the remaining oil over medium heat for a few seconds until crisp and drain on paper towels.
  8. Serve topped with the sliced chestnuts and crisp sage, a trickle of olive oil and plenty of black pepper.

The author notes fresh chestnuts work if blanched, peeled and simmered until tender first.

Tree mallow and lemon soup (molokhia style)

Written for tree mallow (Malva arborea), improvised by the author on molokhia, the Egyptian soup of jute mallow sometimes made with common mallow; the page gives no quantities.

Ingredients
  • Tree mallow leaves, finely chopped
  • water
  • chopped onion
  • oil
  • garlic cloves
  • coriander seeds
  • salt and pepper
  • vegetable stock
  • lemon juice
Method
  1. Purée finely chopped raw tree mallow leaves in a blender with some water.
  2. Fry chopped onion in oil until soft.
  3. Crush garlic cloves, coriander seeds, salt and pepper in a mortar and add them with some vegetable stock and lemon juice, then add the puréed leaves.

The author found tree mallow not very slimy, though the lemon is meant to offset the mucilage; one of the two tasters found it too lemony.

Turkey tail Trametes versicolor 1 recipe

Turkey tail mushroom broth

Makes 2.5 litres

Written for turkey tail with artist's bracket (Ganoderma applanatum) and shiitake.

Ingredients
  • 2 onions with their skins, roughly chopped
  • 1 leek
  • 1 bulb of garlic, halved across
  • 2 celery sticks (ends and tops too)
  • 2 carrots
  • 1 beetroot (optional)
  • an 8 cm piece of fresh ginger, sliced
  • an 8 cm piece of fresh turmeric, sliced (or 30 ml/2 tbsp powder)
  • 50 g dried or fresh mushrooms — turkey tail, artist's bracket pieces and shiitake
  • 8 g dried seaweed (kelp, kombu or wakame)
  • 2.5 ml (½ tsp) crushed black peppercorns
  • 1 large stick of rosemary or 6 thyme sprigs
  • 4 bay leaves
  • 4 litres water
  • 5–10 ml (1–2 tsp) salt
Method
  1. Put everything in a stockpot, bring to the boil uncovered and simmer gently for 1–1½ hours.
  2. Strain out the solids, keeping the mushrooms to slice and return to the liquid.
  3. Bring it back to the boil and bottle it into jars sterilised in a 150 °C oven; the lids pop as they seal.
  4. Store sealed jars in the pantry and opened ones in the fridge.
  5. Drink it as it is, or use it as a base for miso soup or with cooked noodles or rice.

Walnut Juglans regia 3 recipes

Pickled green walnuts

Written for walnuts by New Zealand growers; the page does not name the species.

Ingredients
  • 1 kg fresh green walnuts
  • 250 g salt
  • 2 litres boiling water, in two lots
  • 1 litre malt vinegar
  • 400 g brown sugar
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 1 tsp pickling spice
  • 1 tsp black peppercorns
  • ½ tsp whole cloves
Method
  1. Pick the nuts early, around Christmas, while they are green and before the shell forms: push a sturdy needle through each and throw out any that will not pierce easily.
  2. Wear gloves, as the juice stains skin and is very hard to remove.
  3. Prick the walnuts all over with a fork and put them in a large bowl.
  4. Dissolve half the salt in 1 litre of boiling water, pour it over to cover and leave in a cool place for a week.
  5. Drain, cover with a second brine made the same way and leave another week.
  6. Drain and spread the nuts in one layer on a tray, and set them outside in a sunny spot for 3–4 days, bringing them in at night, until black and dry.
  7. Bring the vinegar, sugar, teaspoon of salt and spices to the boil and simmer about 5 minutes to dissolve the sugar, then cool and strain out the spices.
  8. Bring the liquid back to the boil, pack the walnuts into clean jars and pour it over so every nut is covered.
  9. Cover and keep somewhere dark for at least a month before eating; the growers find them better after 4 months.
  10. Use vinegar-proof lids, or put a layer of cling film between lid and liquid, as vinegar corrodes metal lids and taints the walnuts.

View source recipe

Pork rib and watercress soup

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 500 g meaty pork ribs
  • 1 bunch watercress, washed thoroughly
  • 6 dried Chinese dates, red or black
  • a 2 cm piece of ginger, sliced lengthwise and smashed
  • 2 tsp salt
  • 1 tsp sugar
Method
  1. Cover the ribs with water by about 5 cm in a large pot and bring to a rolling boil, then drain in a colander to get rid of fat and scum and return the ribs to the pot.
  2. Trim the watercress, separate the leaves from the stems and chop the stems small.
  3. Add about 2 litres of water, the watercress stems, dates and ginger and bring to the boil over high heat.
  4. Cover and simmer gently over medium heat for 45 minutes to an hour, until the ribs are tender.
  5. Add the leaves and simmer about 10 minutes more, until they turn dark green.
  6. Stir in the salt and sugar and serve straight away.

View source recipe

Steamed watercress

Serves 4

Written for wild watercress (Nasturtium officinale) by an American chef.

Ingredients
  • 450 g (1 lb) fresh watercress
  • salt
  • soft salted butter or extra virgin olive oil
  • lemon wedges or vinegar, to serve
Method
  1. Wash the watercress, picking out insects and debris, and dry it well, ideally in a salad spinner.
  2. Put a thin film of water in a large pot, fill the pot with the watercress and cover it.
  3. Set it over medium-high heat for a few minutes until the pot is very hot, then lift the lid and stir.
  4. Cover again for a minute or two, stir, and repeat until the watercress has wilted.
  5. Keep cooking and tasting, adding a splash of water if it dries out, until it is tender: young shoots are quick, older leaves can take 15 minutes or more.
  6. Turn off the heat and pour off what little water is left.
  7. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil and salt, taste, and serve with lemon or a dash of vinegar, or butter at the table.

The author also steams it in a steamer basket over 5–8 cm of boiling water, covered on low heat, until tender, but prefers the pot method for watercress.

Watercress and puha salad

The recipe uses raw watercress: use only watercress that is bought or cultivated, or picked from water with no sheep or cattle grazing above it (see this entry's liver fluke warning).

Ingredients
Balsamic reduction (makes about 600 ml; you need 45 ml)
  • 1 litre balsamic vinegar
  • 150 g unrefined cane sugar
  • 1 rosemary stalk
  • half a diced red onion (optional)
Maple walnuts
  • 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts
  • 5 ml (1 tsp) ground cinnamon
  • 30 ml (2 tbsp) maple syrup
  • 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt
Salad (serves 4)
  • half a finely sliced red onion
  • 45 ml (3 tbsp) balsamic reduction
  • 5 ml (1 tsp) salt
  • 1 orange
  • 1 litre (4 cups) watercress
  • 250 ml (1 cup) young puha leaves
  • 4 finely sliced radishes
  • 250 ml (1 cup) sprouts (ruruhau, mizuna, alfalfa or broccoli; optional)
  • 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil
Method
  1. Balsamic reduction: stir until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil, then simmer, stirring often, until reduced by half.
  2. Cool, remove the rosemary and bottle it.
  3. Maple walnuts: toast 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts on a lined tray in a 180 °C oven for 10 minutes, then stir through 5 ml (1 tsp) ground cinnamon, 30 ml (2 tbsp) maple syrup and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and return to the oven for 2 minutes; cool.
  4. Salad: scrunch half a finely sliced red onion with 45 ml (3 tbsp) balsamic reduction and 5 ml (1 tsp) salt in a large bowl and leave it while you prepare the rest, adding each to the bowl without mixing: 1 orange, peeled and segmented; 1 litre (4 cups) watercress, the stems finely chopped (they can be stringy) and the leaves roughly chopped; 250 ml (1 cup) young puha leaves, roughly chopped; 4 finely sliced radishes; and 250 ml (1 cup) ruruhau, mizuna, alfalfa or broccoli sprouts (optional).
  5. Drizzle with 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, add the walnuts, toss and serve.

View source recipe

Watercress and parmesan tart

Fills a 30 cm tart tin

Ingredients
Pastry
  • 125 g very cold butter
  • 250 g sieved plain flour
  • 50 g finely grated parmesan
  • 1 tsp icing sugar
  • salt
  • plenty of black pepper
  • just enough water
Filling
  • 500 g watercress leaves, with some white flowers kept for garnish
  • 20 g butter
  • the juice of 1 orange
  • 3 large eggs plus 2 extra yolks
  • 300 ml double cream
  • 200 g grated parmesan
  • salt and pepper
  • 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180 °C.
  2. For the pastry, grate 125 g very cold butter into 250 g sieved plain flour, 50 g finely grated parmesan, 1 tsp icing sugar, salt and plenty of black pepper.
  3. Rub together lightly, keeping it cool, then add just enough water to form a rough ball (less water, less shrinking).
  4. Chill for 30 minutes, roll out and line the tin, patching where needed.
  5. Prick the base, chill for 20 minutes, then blind-bake with baking paper and beans for 15 minutes; remove them and bake on until lightly toasted.
  6. For the filling, strip 500 g watercress leaves from the fibrous stalks (some stalk is fine — just a coarser tart), keeping some white flowers for garnish.
  7. Melt 20 g butter in a large heavy pan over a medium heat, add the watercress and the juice of 1 orange, and sweat gently for 10 minutes, stirring often.
  8. Blitz it with its juices, then beat it hard with 3 large eggs and 2 extra yolks, 300 ml double cream, all but a handful of 200 g grated parmesan, and plenty of salt and pepper — the more air, the more it rises.
  9. Pour into the case, sprinkle with the reserved parmesan and 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts, and bake for 20–25 minutes, until bronzed and only slightly wobbly in the middle.
  10. Cool a little and scatter the watercress flowers on top.

Watercress soup with carrots

Serves 4

Written for wild watercress by an American chef; the soup is cooked, and the raw sprigs on top follow this entry's preparation.

Ingredients
  • 115 g fresh watercress, chopped (about 4 cups)
  • 1 large floury potato (225 g), peeled and chopped
  • 2 small carrots (115 g), grated
  • 1 medium onion (115 g), chopped
  • 15 g ramp leaves, chopped, or a small garlic clove and a few spring onions
  • 60 g unsalted butter
  • 1 tsp salt
  • about 1 litre chicken or vegetable stock
  • 60 ml dry white wine
  • olive oil, black pepper and a few watercress sprigs, to serve
Method
  1. Sweat the onion, potato and half the carrot in the butter for a few minutes until just tender, without letting the pan colour, then add the wine and cook it off.
  2. Add the stock and salt, bring to the boil, then turn the heat down low and cook for 20 minutes.
  3. Add the watercress and the ramp leaves or garlic and spring onions, and blend with a stick blender, leaving it a little coarse.
  4. Add the rest of the grated carrot and pulse a few times so there are still pieces of carrot and watercress in the soup.
  5. Let it stand a few minutes, or warm it through briefly, so the carrot softens, check the seasoning, and serve with watercress sprigs on top, black pepper and a drizzle of olive oil.

The author's method adds a little sugar with the stock that his list leaves out; ramp leaves are his choice when he has them, garlic and spring onions his stand-in.

Glazed carrots with watercress

Serves 2–4

Written for wild watercress by an American chef, who cooks it partly to rule out liver fluke.

Ingredients
  • 2 large carrots (280 g)
  • 2 very generous handfuls of watercress (115 g), trimmed into small clusters
  • 45 g unsalted butter
  • a handful of chopped ramp leaves or a few sliced spring onions (30 g)
  • 1 tbsp maple syrup or a couple of pinches of sugar
  • a 2.5 cm piece of fresh ginger, finely grated (optional)
  • 240 ml chicken stock or water
  • ½ tsp salt, plus more to taste
Method
  1. Peel the carrots and cut them on the diagonal into 5 mm coins, or halve large ones lengthways first and cut half-moons.
  2. Put the carrots, stock or water, ginger, butter, salt and syrup or sugar in a wide pan, about 30 cm, cover and bring to the boil, then take off the lid and keep cooking.
  3. When the liquid is thick and syrupy and the carrots are tender, lower the heat, keeping the pan from drying out.
  4. Add the watercress and the ramp leaves or spring onions, cover for a few moments to wilt it, then toss, check the seasoning and serve: buttery, salted, and only a little sweet.

The author also makes it with young nettles.

Watercress green omelette

Serves 2

Written for wild watercress by an American chef; the omelette is cooked but the salad on the side is raw, so use watercress that is bought or cultivated, or from water with no sheep or cattle grazing above it (see this entry's liver fluke warning), or serve cooked watercress on the side instead, as the author suggests.

Ingredients

  • 2 large eggs plus 1 yolk

Method
  1. Heat the oven to 150 °C.

  4. Sprinkle on the cheese if using, then put the pan in the oven for a few moments, just to set the top.
  5. Loosen the edge with a spatula, roll the omelette up gently and cut it in two.
  6. Serve on warm plates with the rest of the watercress tossed with lemon juice, the herbs, salt, pepper and oil, and the bacon if using.

The author says the herbs are what make the dish.

Watercress potatoes with smoked kahawai

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 800 g potatoes, peeled and cut into 2 cm slices
  • a small bunch of spring onions, trimmed and sliced
  • 2 bunches of watercress, washed, large stalks removed
  • a splash of flavourless oil
  • 150 g crème fraîche
  • 200 ml skim milk
  • 250 g smoked kahawai or trout, skinned, boned and flaked
  • a squeeze of lemon
  • salt and black pepper
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180 °C.
  2. Simmer the potatoes in a large pan of salted water for 5–7 minutes.
  3. Meanwhile heat a generous splash of oil over a medium-high heat in a lidded pan big enough for the watercress, add the watercress and toss until it starts to wilt, then cover for a minute so the stalks soften.
  4. Uncover, pour in the milk, bring to a simmer, add the crème fraîche, and blend it all in a food processor to a green-flecked sauce.
  5. Drain the potatoes and cool them under cold water so they stop cooking.
  6. Toss them with the sauce, season, and spoon half into a baking dish that holds them all snugly.
  7. Mix the fish with the spring onions and lemon, spread it over the potatoes, cover with the rest of the potatoes and pour over any sauce left.
  8. Bake for 25–30 minutes, until the potatoes are cooked through.

White clover pudding

Ingredients

  • 15 ml (1 tbsp, or one sheet) of unflavoured gelatine
  • 250 ml water
  • 125 ml freshly squeezed orange juice (about two large oranges)
  • 60 ml honey
  • 250 ml cream whipped stiff or 250 ml full-fat Greek yoghurt
  • a pinch of salt
Method
  1. Dissolve the gelatine in 60 ml of water.
  2. In a small saucepan, slowly bring the blossoms, water, orange juice, honey and salt to the boil.
  3. Take it off the heat, stir in the gelatine until it has completely dissolved, and leave it to stand for 10 minutes.
  4. Cover and refrigerate until it begins to set, then fold in the whipped cream or yoghurt, spoon it into a serving bowl and refrigerate until set.

White clover jelly

Ingredients
  • 500 ml–1 litre (2–4 cups) of fresh white clover blossoms, stems removed
  • 1 litre water
  • 60 ml bottled lemon juice (or 1 tsp citric acid)
  • one 50 g box of regular powdered pectin
  • 1.25 kg (5 cups) sugar
Method
  1. Pour the water, just boiled, over the blossoms, push them under and steep for 15–20 minutes.
  2. Strain, pressing the blossoms gently, and top the tea up with water to 1 litre if it is short.
  3. Stir in the lemon juice and bring it to the boil, then whisk in the pectin until it has dissolved and boil hard for a full minute.
  4. Only then add all the sugar at once — added earlier, the jelly will not set — stir until dissolved, return to a full rolling boil for exactly 1 minute, take it off the heat and skim.
  5. Ladle into prepared jars, leaving 5 mm headspace, and process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes.
  6. Cool undisturbed for 12–24 hours before checking the seals; refrigerate any that did not seal, and refrigerate after opening.
  7. Do not leave out the lemon juice: it helps the set and makes the jelly acidic enough to can.

View source recipe

White clover flour

Method
  1. Pick white clover blossoms; leaves and stems can stay in, but they taste stronger, so separate them out for a milder flour.
  2. Pick roughly 8 times the volume you want: it shrinks a lot — about 1 litre of blossoms with stems gave 500 ml of blossoms and about 125 ml of flour.
  3. Lay the blossoms out to dry on a screen somewhere well ventilated and out of direct sun (sun dries them in a few hours, but can cost them nutrients).
  4. Grind them in batches in a small blade coffee grinder, or all at once in a food processor on high for about 5 minutes.
  5. Use it for up to a quarter of the flour in a recipe: it will not hold baked goods together on its own.

The recipe gives a flour that tastes mildly sweet and green, like spring peas, with a spongy texture that suits biscuits and soft baking.

Method

Fennel seed spice

Written for wild fennel in California.

Ingredients
  • Ripe fennel seed heads, dry on the stalk
  • a paper bag
  • a jar
Method
  1. Crush and smell each plant first: fennel smells of aniseed, hemlock smells musty.
  2. Snip off the seed heads carrying the biggest seeds into a paper bag; if they are not quite dry, finish drying them indoors so the seeds do not stick.
  3. At home, strip the seeds from each little cluster with thumb and forefinger into a wide, flat dish.
  4. Pick out the empty clusters, twigs, insects and other debris; tweezers help.
  5. Put the seeds in a jar and freeze for a week to kill any insects or eggs you missed.
  6. Keep them in the spice cupboard, where they last about a year, and use them as you would bought fennel seed.

Wild greens soup

Method

Makes 5 litres

The author uses the flowers only, saying the rest of the plant is toxic; Wikipedia says every part of the plant contains a toxin (not yet checked against this entry). The source does not say which wisteria; Chinese wisteria is the one recorded wild in New Zealand.

Ingredients

  • 750 ml (3 cups) golden sugar

Method
  1. Stir the sugar, water and lemon in a large jar until the sugar dissolves, add the flowers and push them under, leaving room in the jar because the mixture rises and falls as it ferments.

Stir-fried wood ear

Serves 2–4

Written for dried black fungus (wood ear); the page does not name the species.

Ingredients
  • 60 ml (¼ cup) dried wood ear
  • 1 tsp potato starch whisked smooth with 60 ml (¼ cup) cold water
  • 5 eggs
  • 1 tsp sesame oil
  • ½ tsp chicken stock powder or MSG
  • ½ tsp rice wine vinegar
  • 4 tbsp vegetable oil
  • 1 small green capsicum, cut in 3 cm pieces
  • 2 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
  • 3 thin slices ginger
  • 1 tbsp oyster sauce
  • 1 tsp Shaoxing wine
  • 1 tsp soy sauce
  • a good pinch of sugar
Method
  1. Soak the wood ear in hot water for 20 minutes, then drain, squeeze out the excess water, trim off the hard base and tear any large pieces smaller.
  2. Beat the eggs with the sesame oil, stock powder, vinegar and a generous drizzle of the starch slurry.
  3. Heat a wok over medium-high heat with 1 tbsp of the oil and stir-fry the capsicum, wood ear, garlic and ginger until the capsicum softens, then tip onto a plate.
  4. Add the rest of the oil and cook the eggs until barely set.
  5. Return the vegetables with the oyster sauce, Shaoxing wine, soy sauce and sugar, thicken with the remaining slurry, toss and serve straight away.

Hot and sour soup with wood ears

Serves 4

Written for wood ear; the recipe does not name the species.

Ingredients
soup
  • about 950 ml (4 cups) light chicken stock
  • ½ tsp grated ginger
  • a 6 mm slice of galangal (optional)
  • 2 tbsp rice wine vinegar
  • 2 tsp red hot sauce such as sambal or chilli-garlic sauce, or to taste
  • 2 tbsp light-coloured mushroom ketchup, or soy or fish sauce
  • about 55 g small fresh yellowfoot chanterelles, or another fresh mushroom such as buna-shimeji or shiitake

  • 1 large egg, beaten
  • a small handful of sliced spring onions

Method
  1. If using galangal, bruise it with the back of a knife.
  2. Cover dried wood ear with hot water for 15 minutes, then lift it out, discard the soaking water and cut it into 6 mm strips.
  3. Bring all the soup ingredients, mushrooms included, to a simmer and let it bubble gently for 10 minutes.
  4. Stir in the cornflour slurry and the tofu and let it thicken for a minute or two.
  5. Stir the soup briskly clockwise a few times, then drizzle in the egg slowly in the same direction while it is still swirling.
  6. When the egg has set in ribbons, add the spring onions and coriander, divide among four cups and drizzle with chilli oil if you like.
